body_markdown:
When consumers choose a reduced-sugar beverage, lower-sodium snack, high-protein product or no-alcohol cocktail, they still expect it to deliver the taste experience they know and enjoy. That’s where[taste modulation](https://www.iff.com/food-beverage/taste/flavorfit-taste-modulation/) becomes essential.


At IFF, Kees Wisse, Global Innovation Program Director RE-IMAGINE WELLNESS™, helps lead the innovation strategy behind those solutions. His work connects market shifts, customer needs, regional taste expectations and emerging technologies to expand what IFF’s flavorists and product designers can achieve.


“Our role is to enlarge the creative toolbox and, per the RE-IMAGINE WELLNESS™ tagline, ‘advance taste for better living,’” Kees explains. “I know I’m doing my job well when I can put smiles on the faces of our flavorists.”


## **Building the Toolbox Behind Better Taste**


For Kees, his role is part of a broader mission: helping food and beverage manufacturers create products that support[health and wellness goal](https://www.iff.com/food-beverage/health-and-wellness/weight-management/) s without sacrificing enjoyment.


FLAVORFIT ™ solutions span[sugar reduction](https://www.iff.com/food-beverage/taste/flavorfit-taste-modulation/sugar-reduction-solutions/) ,[salt reduction](https://www.iff.com/food-beverage/taste/flavorfit-taste-modulation/salt-reduction-solutions/) , alcohol reduction,[masking](https://www.iff.com/food-beverage/taste/flavorfit-taste-modulation/taste-masking-solutions/) , mouthfeel enhancement,[umami](https://www.iff.com/food-beverage/taste/flavorfit-taste-modulation/umami-flavor/) and sensory effects like cooling or heating sensations.


“Sugar reduction has been around for a long time, and it’s not going away,” Kees says. “Consumers still want sweetness. They still want enjoyment. The challenge is delivering that experience in a new way.”


> “Consumers still want sweetness. They still want enjoyment. The challenge is delivering that experience in a new way.”


That challenge is becoming more complex. Consumers are paying closer attention to calories, sweeteners, sodium levels and ingredient labels. Brands are exploring more natural approaches to formulation while still trying to deliver familiar taste experiences.


The need extends far beyond sweetness, however. Salt reduction continues to gain momentum globally, while functional products often introduce bitterness, dryness or other off-notes that require masking and balancing. Meanwhile, the no- and low-alcohol space continues to expand as consumers seek new experiences that go[beyond traditional alcoholic beverages](https://www.iff.com/media/stories/dry-january-isnt-just-a-pause-its-a-signal/) .


## **Wellness is Changing the Brief**


Through IFF’s[RE-IMAGINE WELLNESS™ program](https://www.iff.com/food-beverage/innovation-programs/) , Kees and his team look at wellness from multiple angles. Physical health remains important, including reducing sugar, salt and alcohol. But wellness also includes enjoyment, emotional satisfaction and creating products consumers genuinely want to return to.


That balance is becoming even more important as consumer behaviors evolve.


For example,[GLP-1 medications are changing](https://www.iff.com/media/stories/how-glp-1-medications-are-rewiring-taste-palates-and-what-it-means-for-fb-innovation/) appetite, portion size, taste perception and nutritional priorities for many consumers. At the same time, brands are developing products with more protein, more fiber, more minerals or vitamins and additional functional benefits. Products like these can create significant taste challenges.


“Consumers may be looking for fewer calories or more nutritional benefits, but they still want joy in eating and drinking,” Kees points out.


As brands rethink sweetness, saltiness, mouthfeel, bitterness and aftertaste, modulation helps make wellness-focused products feel complete rather than compromised.


Kees believes this shift will continue well beyond any single trend.


“More emphasis is being placed on calorie intake, portion size, ingredients and overall health benefits,” he says. “Modulation helps us create foods and beverages that are healthier, enjoyable and affordable.”


## **Global Innovation, Local Relevance**


Kees works from a global perspective, but the sensory details often depend on the market.


[Umami](https://www.iff.com/media/stories/the-fifth-taste-salt-and-fat-take-a-dive-with-umami/) is a perfect example.


In Greater Asia, consumers often prefer a sharp, clean umami taste that appears quickly and fades relatively fast. That preference aligns with many regional cuisines and cooking styles, where preparation times are often shorter.


In parts of Africa, however, consumers may prefer a more lingering umami profile that complements slow-cooked dishes and stews.


“Although we take a global view, we always have to account for local and regional relevance,” Kees explains.


This insight helped inspire a new umami tool developed specifically around the needs of Asian markets. Rather than applying a single global solution everywhere, Kees and his team focus on understanding how consumer expectations differ from region to region.


IFF creative teams around the world serve as the eyes and ears of their regions, bringing forward customer needs and consumer insights that help shape future innovation priorities.


## **Turning Challenges into New Solutions**


Innovation can start from many places. Sometimes it begins with a customer challenge. Other times it comes from changing regulations, shifting consumer expectations or emerging market trends.


For Kees, innovation often starts with a simple question: “What can we do today, and what can we do better tomorrow?”


His team continuously evaluates where new tools are needed and where existing capabilities can be improved. Cost, consumer demand, regulatory requirements and[labeling considerations](https://www.iff.com/food-beverage/clean-label-solutions/) all influence which opportunities move forward.


That process has helped IFF build solutions that support a wide range of customer needs, from high-impact, cost-effective options for emerging markets to clean-label and wellness-focused solutions for more mature markets.


Many of the most successful products rely on multiple modulation technologies working together.


For instance, balancing sweetness perception, masking and mouthfeel is critical, as these often interact in reduced-sugar beverages. Salt reduction tools can work alongside umami solutions in savory applications. In dairy and coffee creamers, texture and flavor perception frequently go hand in hand.


“One tool alone is rarely the full answer,” Kees shares. “The best results come when you understand how they work together.”


Kees recently tasted a snack product where MSG had been replaced and salt reduction technologies were used to create a flavor experience that was not only comparable to the original, but even more appealing.


Sometimes the goal is to replicate a familiar taste as closely as possible. In other situations, innovation can help create an experience consumers enjoy or value that much more.


## **Powered by Collaboration**


Kees describes his role as highly collaborative.


His team works closely with flavorists, designers, R&D teams, marketers, commercial teams and innovation leaders across IFF. Those connections help ensure innovation remains grounded in real customer needs while taking advantage of expertise from across the organization.


“The beauty of IFF is that we are so globally connected,” says Kees. “We can lift and shift ideas, questions and solutions across regions.”


That collaboration extends into IFF’s broader research organization as well. Scientists working in areas such as[food science](https://www.iff.com/science/bioscience/) , botanicals, chemical senses and delivery systems all contribute to the foundation that supports future modulation technologies.


For customers, that integrated approach provides access to expertise that spans disciplines, regions and technologies.


## **The Future of Taste and Wellness**


“Innovation is dreaming big and thinking of crazy, impossible ideas that we really can make possible,” Kees shares.


As new technologies emerge,[including AI-powered tools](https://www.iff.com/food-beverage/digital-flavor-solutions/) and advanced data capabilities, Kees sees opportunities to accelerate innovation while maintaining the creativity and human expertise that define great flavor experiences.


“Our people are always at the heart of what we do,” he says.


For Kees, the future of modulation is not simply about rebalancing sugar, salt or alcohol. It is about helping brands create products that align with changing consumer expectations while preserving the enjoyment that keeps people coming back.


## **Behind the Scenes but Essential**


Kees’ work highlights how taste modulation starts long before a product reaches the shelf. It begins with understanding where consumer expectations are heading, identifying future challenges and developing the tools needed to solve them.


By connecting wellness trends, regional insights and innovation strategy, Kees and his team help ensure flavorists and product designers are equipped for whatever comes next.


> For Kees, innovation starts with a simple question: “What can we do today, and what can we do better tomorrow?”


And while much of that work happens behind the scenes, its impact can be experienced in every product that tastes balanced, satisfying and joyful — even as consumer expectations continue to change.
